title: Gang Suppression Force Formally Launches Full Operations; Force at ~800 Personnel — 15% of Authorized Ceiling — With No Coverage for Cité Soleil or Artibonite
detail: On June 1, 2026, the UN-authorized Gang Suppression Force (GSF) formally launched full operations in Haiti, marking the official transition from the Kenyan-led Multinational Security Support (MSS) mission that concluded with the departure of its final 150 Kenyan officers on April 28, 2026. The June 1 launch represents a statutory mandate milestone — not a deployment milestone. The force on the ground consists of approximately 800 personnel: approximately 400 Chadian troops, ~75 Guatemalan soldiers, and ~70 Salvadoran police officers, under the command of Mongolian Major General Erdenebat Batsuuri (who arrived May 14, 2026). This represents approximately 15% of the 5,500-person authorized ceiling established under UN Security Council Resolution 2793. Chad — the largest contributor — pledged 1,500 personnel by June 2026 and the remainder in subsequent months; full force strength is not expected until fall–end 2026. The GSF's mandate is broader than its predecessor: it can operate independently of the Haitian National Police, conduct intelligence-led anti-gang operations, arrest gang members, seize weapons, secure infrastructure, and support humanitarian access. The critical operational gap on launch day: the advance force remains exclusively deployed in Port-au-Prince's city center corridor. Cité Soleil, Martissant, the Artibonite, the Centre department, and Sud-Est — the zones of most acute gang violence and humanitarian need — have zero GSF coverage. MSF's Cité Soleil hospital, the only health facility accessible to ~300,000 commune residents, enters its 23rd consecutive day of forced closure as of June 1 with no GSF asset in range. The GSF's long-term effectiveness depends on its ability to hold — not merely raid and withdraw from — gang-controlled territory: a lesson from the MSS that never achieved durable territorial rollback despite over 22 months of operations. On the positive side, national pledges to the GSF exceed its 5,500-person authorized ceiling, with $200M+ pledged by 13 states and $59M disbursed; Qatar pledged $30M in April 2026.

title: MSF Partially Resumes Port-au-Prince Activities as Cité Soleil Hospital Enters Day 23 of Forced Closure
detail: As of June 1, 2026 — the same day the Gang Suppression Force formally launched full operations — MSF (Doctors Without Borders) announced it had partially resumed medical activities in Port-au-Prince following the acute violence of mid-May. However, the MSF hospital in Cité Soleil — the only health facility accessible to the commune's approximately 300,000 residents who live entirely under gang control — enters its 23rd consecutive day of forced closure, matching the longest documented uninterrupted shutdown of a major healthcare facility in Cité Soleil since the 2021 crisis began. The forced closure began May 10, 2026 when intense intra-Viv Ansanm gang fighting between Chen Mechan/Taliban/400 Mawozo factions and Duvivier/Pyè 6 factions erupted in Cité Soleil and the Cul-de-Sac Plain. MSF teams had treated over 40 gunshot wound patients in 12 hours before evacuating; 800+ displaced civilians had sheltered inside the compound. An MSF security guard was struck by a stray bullet inside the facility. The partial resumption of activities in other Port-au-Prince neighborhoods does not restore emergency, trauma, or maternal care to Cité Soleil. UN monitoring indicates approximately 30,000+ people remain newly displaced since May 10 in the commune and surrounding areas, adding to the 1.5 million national IDP total. The fundamental conditions preventing Cité Soleil access — gang territorial control of the commune with no GSF presence — remain unchanged as of June 1. The GSF advance force's exclusive concentration in the city center corridor means that securing Cité Soleil, if it occurs, depends on a sequential expansion of the force that is not expected until well into fall 2026.
